articleHeadline: Avian Influenza in China: Research reveals barriers to human transmission
articleSummary: As of March 2026, avian influenza H5N1 has devastated poultry populations in China, resulting in the death of tens of millions of chickens and turkeys, and has recently affected dairy cattle. Despite the virus's ability to enter human cells, human cases remain extremely rare due to robust cellular defenses. Key findings from Zhejiang University indicate that the STING pathway plays a crucial role in triggering antiviral responses, limiting viral replication. Experiments show that the absence of STING or GADD34, a gene activated by STING, leads to increased viral levels and more severe disease in lab mice and human lung cells. Notably, over 95% of human pandemic strains carry a mutation in the avian M1 matrix protein that suppresses STING signaling, highlighting the complexity of the virus's transmission dynamics and potential therapeutic targets. Current research emphasizes the importance of understanding these barriers to prevent future outbreaks.
